name: double-dispatch
intent: Select the operation to execute from the runtime types of two collaborating objects, so behaviour can vary along two independent type axes instead of being resolved by hand-written type tests in the caller.
problem: Behaviour depends on the runtime type of *two* objects - element and visitor, shape and surface, left operand and right operand - but an ordinary call resolves on the receiver only (or, in dynamic languages, on no argument at all). Every operation then grows its own type-test ladder, knowledge of the concrete classes leaks into callers, and adding a class silently breaks the cases nobody remembered to extend.
context: Object models in which two type hierarchies interact: shape x medium, AST node x operation, operand x operand, entity x entity in a collision matrix. It applies when the pair-specific behaviour is a real matrix rather than a single special case, when each hierarchy evolves on its own schedule, and when the language's own dispatch resolves only one of the two runtime types (classic single-dispatch OO) or none of them (method overloading is bound statically).
benefits: Pair-specific behaviour is selected by the dispatch mechanism instead of by explicit type tests, so the operation code never inspects types.
Operations stay open for extension: a new visitor, table entry or match arm adds behaviour without touching either element hierarchy.

Coverage becomes checkable: a visitor interface with one method per concrete type, or an exhaustive match over a closed hierarchy, turns a forgotten pair into a compile error rather than a runtime surprise.
Knowledge of the concrete type set is centralised in one place (the visitor interface, the dispatch table, the sealed hierarchy), which makes the N x M matrix auditable.
Symmetric and asymmetric pairs can be expressed deliberately - commutative pairs canonicalised once - instead of being rediscovered at each call site.
The first dispatch already knows the concrete receiver type, so the second handler receives statically typed operands with no casts or RTTI lookups.

Provides a compile-time todo list when the hierarchy grows: every concrete visitor must implement the new visit method or the build fails — the pattern converts silent runtime no-ops into loud compile errors.
tradeoffs: The pair matrix grows as the product of the two hierarchies: N x M cases, or N*(N+1)/2 when commutative pairs are canonicalised, so every new type multiplies the work.
Classic double dispatch is intrusive: every element class gains an accept (or equivalent) method, coupling the data model to the operation set.

The second dispatch fixes the overload set at compile time, so the visitor must name every concrete element type; an overload for the base type or a default arm removes exactly the check that makes the pattern worthwhile.

Dynamic-resolution forms (C# dynamic, Python/JS pair tables, string-built Ruby selectors) trade compile-time coverage for a runtime lookup: failures move to runtime, and caching adds memory-leak surface.
Two virtual calls or a hash lookup per pair make dispatch measurably more expensive than a single virtual call, which matters in tight numeric or collision loops.
Commutative pairs encoded twice drift apart, and asymmetric pairs that look symmetric produce order-dependent bugs.
The visitor/element dependency cycle couples the two hierarchies: forward declarations help but never eliminate the mutual dependency.

std::variant + std::visit adds lambda-capture overhead (extra stores/loads per call) compared to virtual dispatch on simple strategies — on GCC/libstdc++ this can be 28-30% slower in microbenchmarks, though GCC 12+ added a fast switch path for small variants.

participants.responsibility: Owns the entry-point dispatch method (accept, collideWith, renderOn) and determines the first axis of the pair through its runtime type.
Determines the second axis; must provide one callback per receiver type (visitCircle, collideWithCircle) so the pair can be identified.
A virtual call on the receiver — or a type switch where there is no virtual dispatch — that pins the receiver's concrete type.
A call on the argument carrying the receiver, whose overload resolution or dynamic method lookup pins the argument's concrete type; after it both types are statically or dynamically known.
The code for exactly one cell of the matrix: a concrete visitor method, a table entry or one match arm per (receiver type, argument type).
A registry or table keyed by the two types (type-index map, multimethod object) that resolves the pair without adding a method to either hierarchy.

use_cases: Collision and interaction rules in games and simulations: every pair of entity types (bullet × wall, ship × asteroid) has its own outcome. Double dispatch cleanly selects the correct collision algorithm at runtime. Used in Unity, Unreal, and custom game engines via visitor-like hierarchies or type-indexed collision matrices. Spatial partitioning (quad-trees, oct-trees) is used alongside to reduce O(n²) pair checks. Examples: Unity physics collision callbacks, Unreal collision/overlap event system, Box2D physics engine, custom engines with AABB/Sphere/OBB hierarchies.

Geometry predicates between two shape hierarchies: intersect, contains, distance and other predicates where each pair (circle-circle, circle-rectangle, rectangle-rectangle) uses a different algorithm and pairs are not symmetric. Used in game physics engines, computer graphics rendering pipelines, and GIS systems. Examples: Box2D, Chipmunk, computer graphics rendering engines.

Numeric promotion and operator semantics between unrelated numeric types: Rational × Integer, Money × Currency, BigInt × Float — operations that must consult both operands' concrete types. Ruby's Numeric#coerce is the canonical language mechanism enabling this pattern. Examples: Ruby Numeric#coerce, Java BigDecimal arithmetic, C# decimal/float/double mixed arithmetic.

Document rendering and media output: shapes or widgets × output targets (screen, printer, PDF, HTML), where each combination emits different code. The medium axis and the shape type axis independently determine the rendering path. Examples: Qt/wxWidgets painting systems, Java AWT/Swing paint(Graphics) dispatch, WebKit/Blink layout engines.

AST traversal and transformations: one node hierarchy × many analyses (type check, pretty-print, evaluate, optimise) — the primary use case the Visitor pattern was designed for. Each (Operation × NodeType) pair is a separate handler. Examples: Babel/TypeScript compiler, LLVM compiler infrastructure, Roslyn C# compiler API.

Plugin and extension architectures: a host application defines an element hierarchy and a plugin defines a visitor; new plugins add operations without modifying element classes. Examples: Eclipse IDE plugin system, Visual Studio Analyzer/extension APIs, static analysis tools (linters, formatters).

Serialization and deserialization frameworks: Format (JSON, XML, binary, protobuf) × type — each combination may need different encoding rules. Examples: Jackson/Gson in Java, Python dataclasses serialization, Protocol Buffers schema evolution.

Protocol handling in parsers and state machines: handler depends on both message kind and connection/session kind — a state × event matrix. Used in network protocol stacks, parsers, and finite state machine implementations. Examples: HTTP server request routing, game AI state machines, telecom protocol state tables.

Event handling in GUI frameworks: a widget hierarchy × an event hierarchy (mouse, keyboard, focus) — each (Widget × Event) pair may require different handling logic. The classic AWT/Swing processEvent double-dispatch was the motivating example for several academic multi-dispatch papers. Examples: Java AWT event delegation, Qt event handling, Swing ActionMap/InputMap.

Message routing in game architectures: entity × message type routing where the correct handler depends on both the receiver entity's type and the message's payload type. Common in Entity-Component-System (ECS) patterns where components process messages differently. Examples: Unity MessageSystem, Amazon Lumberyard (component × message routing).

Numeric and array operators as native multiple dispatch: Julia makes the pair axis first-class - arithmetic and promotion operators are generic functions whose methods select on the runtime types of all arguments, and the compiler emits a specialised version per concrete combination (Int,Int vs Float64,Float64) instead of a hand-rolled accept/visit round-trip; promote_type absorbs cross-type cells. The canonical modern realisation of the pattern. Examples: Julia Base arithmetic, Julia promote_type/coercion, heterogeneous-array dispatch costs documented in the Julia performance guide.

Generic functions in CLOS and Dylan-family languages: method selection keyed by the classes or identities of every required argument, with method combination (call-next-method) resolving ambiguity - double dispatch without the intrusive accept method, and the benchmark every manual encoding is measured against. Examples: ANSI Common Lisp CLOS defgeneric/defmethod, Dylan generic functions.

Runtime binder dispatch on the CLR: the C# dynamic keyword defers overload resolution to the Dynamic Language Runtime, binding the call on the runtime types of receiver and arguments with call-site caching; CallSiteBinder.Bind is documented as runtime binding (double-dispatch). A missing pair surfaces as a runtime binder exception rather than a compile error, so it suits dynamic-language and COM interop boundaries more than closed business matrices. Examples: DLR call-site caching, IronPython/IronRuby interop, COM interop via the runtime binder.
avoid_when: Only one axis actually varies: single dispatch, a Strategy or a plain function parameter is simpler and needs no second hierarchy.
Both hierarchies are closed and you own them: the language's exhaustive match (sealed + switch, enum + match, discriminated union) covers both axes with less machinery.
The pair set is small and stable: a switch on a tag field, or a lookup keyed by two enum values, is the dispatch table you actually need.
You need three or more axes: triple dispatch multiplies the matrix again and is almost always beaten by composing two binary steps (Fowler reports abandoning the one triple-dispatch design he tried).

The operation is already expressible as a protocol or a canonicalised symmetric key: numeric coercion (coerce), operator overloading or sorting the pair before a single lookup removes the need for a second hierarchy.
The types are only known from untrusted input: dispatching on types that arrive from outside without validating them replaces a modelling problem with a security one.

The element hierarchy changes frequently while operations are stable: each new element type requires updating the visitor interface and every concrete visitor — better to invert the dependency and use a dispatch table that throws at runtime for unregistered pairs.
anti_patterns: Type-test ladders (instanceof / typeid / type-switch chains): the absence of this pattern's dispatch mechanism — each operation grows its own branching chain, concrete type knowledge leaks into callers, and adding a new type silently breaks forgotten branches. Replace the ladder with a visitor or dispatch table so the compiler reports missing cells.

Visitor with a catch-all default or base-type overload: implementing a visit(Shape) or visit(BaseType) method that throws at runtime, while claiming the compile-time coverage the pattern provides. Keep the second dispatch total with abstract-only visit methods so link-time errors catch missing implementations.

String-built selectors (send('visit_' + className)): dispatch keyed by class name strings — slow, invisible to refactoring tools, and unsafe when the name can be influenced by untrusted input. Use language-native type dispatch or an explicit type-to-handler map.
Asymmetric pair handling: encoding both (A,B) and (B,A) separately so symmetric behaviour drifts apart over time. Canonicalise the pair before lookup and share one implementation for symmetric pairs.

Single-dispatch with a type test called 'double dispatch': one axis resolved by polymorphism, the other by an explicit if/instanceof chain — still leaves type knowledge in the operation. Use two successive dispatches rather than one dispatch plus branching.

Using double dispatch for a two-way decision that a canonical ordering plus one comparison would settle: applying the full pattern where a simple comparator (Ruby's <=>, sorting the pair) would be cheaper and clearer. Check whether the operation is genuinely a matrix or a single comparison suffices.

Open type hierarchies with a closed dispatch table: when the element hierarchy is open but the dispatch table is closed, unregistered types fail at runtime. Use the classic Visitor with abstract visit methods so new elements fail at link time, or use a register-based table with an explicit 'unregistered type' error.
Mutable shared state between pair handlers: makes traversal order observable and reentrancy unsafe. Always return a value from handlers instead of writing to shared state.

dynamic_cast as a substitute for double dispatch: dynamic_cast chains are O(N) in the hierarchy depth, silently fall through when the throw branch is omitted, and require editing every operation when a new type is added. A single double dispatch replaces an entire dynamic_cast chain with two virtual calls — measured as 7.5× faster in microbenchmarks.

Premature generalisation to triple dispatch: the N×M×L matrix explodes and the dispatch chain becomes unreadable. Compose two binary dispatches instead. Fowler abandoned his one triple-dispatch attempt; Bjarne Stroustrup noted the same in his open-methods proposal.
design_principles: Open/closed principle along the operations axis: new operations arrive as visitors, table entries or match arms, not as edits to the element classes.
Single responsibility: each pair handler implements exactly one cell of the matrix, and the dispatch method only dispatches.
Dependency inversion: element classes depend on an abstract visitor or dispatcher role instead of on concrete operations.
Separation of concerns: deciding which code runs (dispatch) is kept apart from what the code does (behaviour).
Tell, don't ask: the receiver is asked to dispatch rather than interrogated about its type.
Fail loudly: the absence of a handler must be a compile error or an explicit runtime exception — never a silent no-op.
best_practices: Decide which axis grows faster and put it on the visitor/table side; keep the stable axis in the element classes to minimise changes to both hierarchies.
Keep the second dispatch total — no overload for the base type, no default arm — so the compiler reports unhandled cells and adding a new type produces a compile error, not a silent runtime no-op.
Canonicalise commutative pairs (A × B and B × A) before lookup so symmetric behaviour has exactly one implementation and the matrix collapses to a triangle.
Return a value from the pair handler instead of writing into shared state, so handlers stay testable, reentrant and parallel-safe.

Prefer the language's exhaustive match (sealed class + switch, enum + match, discriminated union) when both hierarchies are closed, and reserve the classic visitor for open or third-party hierarchies.
Test the whole grid (or the canonicalised triangle) from a table-driven test built from the type list, not from hand-written cases — this catches missing cells automatically as the type set grows.
Do not generalise past two axes: compose two binary dispatches instead of writing triple dispatch (Fowler abandoned his one triple-dispatch attempt).

For closed type sets in C++, prefer std::variant + std::visit over the classic two-vtable Visitor — benchmarks show ~2–4× higher throughput and better inlining for small type sets; use the classic Visitor for open hierarchies with externally contributed types. Note: on GCC/libstdc++ there is ~28% lambda-capture overhead vs virtual dispatch in microbenchmarks; profile before selecting for hot paths.

In Python, use functools.singledispatch as the first dispatch layer; combine with explicit type checks inside registered implementations for the second axis, or use the multipledispatch library for true double dispatch.

In C++, prefer Style B naming (visitCircle, visitRectangle — named per concrete type) over Style A (overloaded visit(Shape&)) — Style B produces a compile error for missing overloads, Style A silently falls through.
In C++, use pure virtual (= 0) declarations for every visit method on the Visitor base — not default empty bodies — so incomplete concrete visitors fail to compile rather than silently link.
In C++, store visitors by value or by shared_ptr, never by raw reference across scope boundaries where the referent's lifetime may end before the dispatcher fires.
In performance-sensitive loops (game physics, rendering), construct the dispatcher outside the loop and cache the result — storing a visitor by value in a hot loop adds measurable overhead.

Use the pattern as the dispatch mechanism, not as a substitute for good data design: if the two axes represent genuinely separate concerns, double dispatch is correct; if it papers over a modelling problem, refactor toward separate data and operations.

When adding a new type to an open hierarchy, update the visitor interface first (add the new visit method signature), then implement it in every concrete visitor — a missing implementation is a link-time or compile-time error with abstract-base enforcement.

When both hierarchies are owned and stable, consider whether the pattern is needed at all: an enum-keyed dispatch table or a sealed class + exhaustive match is simpler, faster to write, and still fails at compile time when a pair is unhandled.
For JavaScript/TypeScript, avoid string-keyed dispatch (constructor.name or string concatenation) — use a Symbol-keyed Map or a frozen object table so minification does not break dispatch.

In Go, consider whether a simple interface with a method per operation (not Visitor) is sufficient before adding the full accept/visit round-trip — Go's structural typing makes the visitor interface contract impossible to enforce at compile time.

related_patterns_notes.visitor: visitor: Visitor is the canonical packaging of double dispatch for single-dispatch languages — the accept() method is the first dispatch, the visit() overload is the second. Double dispatch is the mechanism; Visitor is the named pattern.
related_patterns_notes.acyclic-visitor: Breaks the cycle between visitor and element hierarchies by using interface decoupling, preserving the double-dispatch mechanism while removing the mutual dependency.
related_patterns_notes.dispatch-table: A table keyed by (Type1, Type2) → handler provides the same dispatch without adding methods to either hierarchy. Replaces the two-method round-trip with a single hash lookup or array index.
related_patterns_notes.sealed-hierarchy-exhaustive-match: Language-native exhaustive pattern matching (sealed class + match/switch, discriminated union) covers both dispatch axes without visitor boilerplate when both hierarchies are closed and owned.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy encapsulates a single family of algorithms; used together with double dispatch when the second axis is the 'which algorithm' axis. Double dispatch selects which strategy to use.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: Defines an algorithm skeleton with hook methods; can compose with double dispatch where the first dispatch fills in a step and the second dispatch selects a concrete algorithm variant.
related_patterns_notes.type-erasure: Type erasure (std::any, Java Object, Python typing) hides the second axis behind a common interface; double dispatch then resolves concrete types at runtime.
related_patterns_notes.command: Command encapsulates a request as an object; when commands are parameterised by the receiver type, a two-level dispatch (command creation then execution) can be combined with double dispatch for complex routing.
related_patterns_notes.multimethod: Language-native multiple dispatch (CLOS, Dylan, Julia) performs double dispatch in a single language-level call; double dispatch in single-dispatch languages simulates this capability. Note: multimethod refers to the language feature; double dispatch is the idiomatic simulation of that feature in languages without it.
related_patterns_notes.factory: Factory method or abstract factory can be combined with double dispatch where the factory selects which concrete product to create based on two type tags, then the product uses double dispatch internally for its behaviour.
related_patterns_notes.mediator: A mediator can coordinate double dispatch by holding references to both hierarchies and routing calls, effectively externalising the accept() round-trip into a separate object rather than embedding it in the element hierarchy.
